text: Resources now live in the cloud, reachable over the open internet, and users connect from anywhere — so access still has to be gated by something. What fills that role is identity. Strong identity verification, not network location, is what actually decides whether access is granted. The checkpoint moved from the network edge to the sign-in itself.

Under the old gate, being inside the corporate network was often enough. Under the new gate, network location no longer matters at all — what matters is whether the identity making the request can be verified, through strong authentication like MFA, regardless of where that request physically came from. That's the real meaning of identity being the new perimeter.

Under castle-and-moat, the firewall was the primary defense, and an attacker still had to get past internal protections behind it. In an identity-perimeter world, the sign-in is usually the primary defense by itself. A set of correct credentials, typed in from anywhere on earth, is often enough to reach a cloud resource directly — there's no network layer left behind it to catch a mistake.

That's exactly why IAM and MFA stopped being 'one more control' and became the front line. IAM decides which identities can access which resources, and with how much privilege. MFA ensures a stolen password alone isn't enough to defeat that decision. And this still connects to least privilege access and verify explicitly — identity gets checked on every request, not trusted for the rest of a session just because the first check passed.

Think of a cloud HR system with a public internet address and no corporate network to be inside of at all. The only thing standing between an outsider and payroll data is the sign-in page — who this is, how strongly they proved it, and whether their role actually warrants access. Next up: what happens after that sign-in, when verification has to keep running for the rest of the session.
